events.answer:
**Urgency: routine, based on what you've shared so far.** The urgency check found no emergency pattern. That is not a clearance. It only means your description didn't match its fixed list. If your low mood gets worse, or you have any thoughts of harming yourself, please contact a doctor, crisis line, or emergency services right away. Don't wait for a scheduled appointment.

**Red flags I could not check.** Your question asked about self-harm thoughts, not being able to function, and substance use. The safety check did not flag any of these, but my search for guidance on them failed, so I can't tell you what the reference material says about them. If any of these apply to you, please speak to a clinician or crisis service soon.

**What might be worth raising with a clinician.** The reference material I could access does not describe persistent low mood or depression directly. It lists a few conditions that can share some features. Each is only something to ask about, and none is a diagnosis:
- **An underactive thyroid** can cause low mood, fatigue, and slowed thinking. It is confirmed with repeated blood tests.
- **Iron-deficiency anemia** can cause fatigue and reduced energy, and is often found on a routine blood count.
- **Insomnia** lasting three months or more can contribute to low mood, and sleep patterns are a key part of its assessment.
- **Generalized anxiety disorder** requires worry on most days for six months, so it does not fit a four-month pattern on its own, but a clinician may still ask about anxiety.

**Details that would change how urgent this is:**
- Any thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life, or thoughts that you would be better off dead.
- Whether you can still work, study, look after yourself, or manage daily tasks.
- Changes in sleep, appetite, weight, energy, or concentration.
- Whether you still enjoy things you used to enjoy.
- Whether you have been using alcohol, cannabis, or other substances more than usual, or taking any medicines you have recently started or stopped.
- Whether anything physical has changed, such as weight, cold intolerance, constipation, or heavy periods.
- Whether the low mood is getting worse, staying the same, or coming and going.

A doctor can help work out the cause and what to do next. If you can, book an appointment soon and bring a note of the answers to these questions.

events.answer:

It flagged the phrase as I wrote it in the check, so it does not confirm that you have these thoughts. Still, please answer this directly: **are you having thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life?**

- In the United States, you can call or text **988** (Suicide and Crisis Lifeline) at any time. Other countries have equivalent services.
- If you are not in immediate danger but are having these thoughts, contact a crisis line or a doctor the same day. Do not wait for a routine appointment.

**What the reference material says.** The guidance I could access describes thoughts of suicide as a reason to reach help immediately (red-flag-suicidal-ideation). **Possible medical causes a clinician may want to rule out.** These come from the general clinical reference. They are questions to ask, not diagnoses:
- **Underactive thyroid** (condition-hypothyroidism). Low mood and slowed thinking can occur, usually alongside tiredness, cold intolerance, weight change, or constipation. It is confirmed with repeated blood tests.
- **Insomnia** (condition-insomnia). Sleep problems lasting three months or more can reduce enjoyment and energy. A sleep diary helps assess this.
- **Generalized anxiety disorder** (condition-generalized-anxiety-disorder). Persistent worry can come with low mood. It requires worry on most days for six months, so it does not fit a four-month pattern on its own.

**Medication effects** were not covered by the guidance I could retrieve. If you take any medicines, or have recently started or stopped one, tell a clinician or pharmacist. Do not change any medicine on your own.

**Please tell a clinician:**

events.answer:
**Urgency: routine, but the earlier emergency screen still applies.** The urgency check for your full description found no emergency pattern. That is not a clearance. Your earlier message about not enjoying things was screened as an emergency. If you have any thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life, contact a crisis line such as **988** in the United States, or your local emergency number, now. Do not wait for a routine appointment.

**Poor sleep.** The reference material describes insomnia as difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking early, together with daytime problems such as tiredness or low mood (condition-insomnia). Short-term poor sleep is common and often passes. Chronic insomnia is defined as sleep problems on at least three nights a week for at least three months (guideline-insomnia-cbt-first-line). You have described about four months of low mood, so a clinician may want to ask how often your sleep is poor and for how long. A sleep diary kept for one to two weeks is one way to do this.

**Symptoms grouped by body system.** The grouping tool found no recognized pattern, so I can't name a body system from its output. Based on what you've written, these are the areas involved:
- **Mood and thinking:** low mood, reduced enjoyment.
- **Sleep:** poor sleep.

No other symptoms have been described, so I can't say whether more than one body system is involved.

**Questions to take to a clinician.** These are not diagnoses:
- Underactive thyroid (condition-hypothyroidism) can cause low mood, tiredness, and slowed thinking. It is confirmed with repeated blood tests.
- Insomnia (condition-insomnia) is assessed partly by looking at sleep patterns over time.
- Iron-deficiency anemia (condition-iron-deficiency-anemia) can cause tiredness and is often found on a routine blood count.
- Generalized anxiety disorder (condition-generalized-anxiety-disorder) can include disturbed sleep and difficulty concentrating, but it requires six months of worry, so it does not fit four months on its own.

The reference material did not cover depression or sleep problems linked to medicines, alcohol, or other substances. Please tell a clinician about any of these.

events.question: I am waking about four in the morning.
events.answer:
**Urgency: routine for the 4 a.m. waking on its own, but the earlier emergency screen still applies.** The urgency check found no emergency pattern for waking at 4 a.m. That is not a clearance. Your earlier message about not enjoying things was flagged as an emergency. If you have any thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life, contact **988** in the United States, your local crisis line, or your local emergency number now.

**Red flags to check for.** The reference material describes these as needing urgent assessment rather than a routine appointment (condition-copd). The source describes them in the context of lung disease, but the symptoms themselves are general:
- Chest pain.
- Breathlessness, especially at rest or getting worse.
- Confusion or unusual drowsiness.
- Blue lips or fingers.

If any of these happen when you wake, seek emergency care. Also tell a clinician if you wake with a headache most mornings, or if someone tells you that you snore loudly or stop breathing during sleep. The reference material treats these as reasons for assessment (lifestyle-migraine-sleep).

**Possible causes a clinician may want to check.** These are questions to ask, not diagnoses:
- **Sleep disruption from habits.** Alcohol, caffeine, and nicotine can all cause early waking. Alcohol is noted as a common cause of early waking (lifestyle-insomnia-sleep).
- **Mood changes.** The guidance lists depression among the conditions that commonly present as insomnia, so a clinician would screen for it (guideline-insomnia-cbt-first-line). I could not retrieve passages specifically on early waking in depression.
- **Medicines.** Medication effects are listed as something to review in insomnia assessment (guideline-insomnia-cbt-first-line). Tell a clinician or pharmacist about any medicines you take or have recently started or stopped. Do not change them yourself.
- **Sleep-disordered breathing.** Obstructive sleep apnea is listed as a condition to screen for in insomnia assessment (guideline-insomnia-cbt-first-line). It is confirmed by a clinician, often with a sleep study.

**Details that would sharpen the assessment:**
- How long the 4 a.m. waking has happened, and how many nights a week.
- Whether you fall back asleep, and how long you stay awake.
- Whether you snore, or someone has seen you stop breathing in your sleep.
- Whether you wake with a headache, or feel very sleepy during the day.
- Your alcohol, caffeine, and nicotine use, especially in the evening.
- Any medicines you take.
- Whether you have any thoughts of harming yourself.

A sleep diary kept for one to two weeks is a useful next step, and the guidance recommends it for assessment (guideline-insomnia-cbt-first-line). Please book a GP or primary-care appointment soon and bring the diary and your answers.
